weeks.title: Schema first — ingest without inventing columns

lesson.title: Schema first — ingest without inventing columns
lesson.body_md:
A dashboard begins with a question and a declared unit of observation. In the Pier Ledger teaching fixture, each row is one fictional count observation at a named bay and time. A headcount is not a unique visitor identity, so adding counts across times does not establish how many different people visited. Before analysis, declare which fields the source really contains and which question they can support.

A CSV header is a sequence of column names. It does not enforce types or uniqueness. This exercise expects visit_id, pier_bay, ts_utc, headcount and source_file, in that order. The parser checks exact columns and row width, then validates identifiers, known aliases and timestamps. It rejects extra columns rather than assuming they are harmless. Integers arrive as text and need validation before arithmetic.

## Guided practice

Download all four Pier Ledger learner resources and follow their README commands. `case_data.py visits.csv` creates six original fictional rows. `ledger.py visits.csv report.json` reads actual bytes and creates evidence. Expected result: rows_in is 6 and rows_out is 4. Open the CSV and count manually before reading the report. source_sha256 identifies the exact bytes; it does not prove their accuracy or ownership.

Save a copy, change v1's count from 20 to 21, and regenerate under a new output name. Expected result: the hash changes, but row counts do not. If your hash differs only because line endings changed, explain that byte identity and equivalent table meaning are different tests.

## Independent evidence and recovery

Declare the observation unit, schema, raw count and file hash for an instructor-issued case. Include a rejected extra-column example. Preserve the original input if validation fails; inspect delimiters and filename extensions rather than inventing missing fields. The historical lab_schema_ingest checks a declared artifact shape and broad constraints; it does not itself read a CSV or independently verify its hash. Use the new computed report and reviewer inspection for source-bound evidence. Neither a self-reported hash nor a successful practice run establishes mastery.

## Runnable resources

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: Six raw fictional rows contain one missing and one negative count. The computed report retains four rows and hashes the actual bytes. A changed count changes the hash; a declaration alone does not verify provenance.

weeks.title: SQL SELECT with pier filters — honest predicates

lesson.title: SQL SELECT with pier filters — honest predicates
lesson.body_md:
SQL SELECT describes which columns and rows to retrieve. FROM names a table; WHERE filters individual rows. A predicate is a condition that evaluates for each row. `headcount > 40` excludes a count of exactly 40, whereas `>= 40` includes it. Query semantics must match the question before a chart is designed.

The runnable example creates an in-memory SQLite table from validated observations. Parameter placeholders separate a query's fixed structure from its threshold value. This is a local authored program, not a service for executing arbitrary visitor SQL. An ordered result makes comparisons reproducible; without ORDER BY, row order should not be assumed.

## Guided practice

Run the Pier Ledger example at thresholds 40 and 60 with different output filenames. Read the actual SQL in ledger.py: it selects visit_id and headcount where headcount is strictly greater than a bound value, then orders by visit_id. Expected result: v3=60 and v4=80 for 40; only v4=80 for 60. At 100 the selected list is empty. Empty selection is an accurate answer, not necessarily a pipeline failure.

Notice that the overall mean remains 50 in all three reports. That KPI is computed over all cleaned rows, not just the selection. Name the population for every number so a reader can interpret it. A WHERE clause can silently change that population if moved into a summary query.

## Independent evidence and recovery

Predict results for a different threshold before running your own query. Include an exactly-at-threshold case and a no-match case. Temporarily change `>` to `>=` in a copy; the public SQL contract test must detect the defect. Restore the predicate and rerun. The old lab_sql_select checks declaration fields and query text; text containing WHERE is not proof that a query executed correctly. Preserve SQL, source identity, predicted row IDs and actual output for review.

## Runnable resources

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: Strict headcount > 40 selects v3=60 and v4=80. With > 60 only v4 remains. The whole-cleaned-population mean stays 50 because this query does not redefine that KPI.

weeks.title: Normalize and transform — clean before KPI

lesson.title: Normalize and transform — clean before KPI
lesson.body_md:
Normalization maps different representations of the same intended key to a canonical value. It is a policy, not a license to merge any similar-looking labels. This fixture explicitly maps Bay-A, bay_a and BAY A to bay_a, and Bay-B and bay_b to bay_b. An unknown label is rejected for review so a spelling guess cannot silently move an observation.

Missing, zero and invalid values differ. A missing headcount says the count is unavailable. Zero is an observed count of none under the fixture's rules. A negative count is invalid in this model. Replacing missing with zero would change the question and bias a mean downward. Dropping invalid rows also changes the analyzed population and must be reported.

## Guided practice

Trace all six CSV rows. Four rows with counts 20, 40, 60 and 80 remain. v5 is rejected as missing and v6 as negative. Expected result: missing_rate_raw is 1/6, using every raw row as the denominator; rows_out is 4. The negative row is excluded from the missing numerator. Do not use the cleaned denominator for this defined metric.

In a copy change v1's count to 0. Expected result: four valid rows remain and the mean becomes 45. Change it to an empty cell instead: only three valid rows remain. Explain why those transformations cannot be substituted for each other. Inspect the rejected list to follow each excluded row.

## Independent evidence and recovery

For a new case, produce a row-accounting table with raw, retained and rejected counts and reasons. Define any normalization extension before using it. Test an unknown alias, a negative count, zero and a missing value. Keep rejected source bytes and explain a legitimate repair rather than deleting an inconvenient record. The legacy validator's declared normalization flags do not independently establish that a transformation was performed.

## Runnable resources

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: Missing=1 of 6 raw rows, so missing_rate_raw=1/6. Negative=1 separately. Retained values 20,40,60,80. Replacing 20 with zero retains four rows and changes the mean to 45.

lesson.title: KPI calc — arithmetic before tiles (NO_AI)
lesson.body_md:
A key performance indicator is a defined summary chosen to address a question. The arithmetic mean adds values and divides by their count. Its denominator matters: the mean of four valid observations differs from the mean after treating two invalid observations as zero. State exclusions alongside the result.

A percentile requires a convention. This lab defines nearest-rank p95: sort n valid values in ascending order and choose the value at one-based rank ceil(0.95*n). For four values the rank is 4, so p95 is the maximum. Other software can interpolate instead; a difference is not automatically a bug until methods are aligned. Four observations are too few for a stable characterization of a real population tail.

## Guided practice — calculate before running

The valid counts are 20, 40, 60 and 80. Their sum is 200; mean is 200/4=50. Sorted order is unchanged; ceil(0.95*4)=4, so nearest-rank p95=80. Expected result: the computed report matches both 50 and 80. Compare with your calculations. There are three bay_a observations averaging 40 and one bay_b observation of 80. The unweighted mean of those two group means is 60, which is not the all-observation mean. Weighting group means by counts restores 50.

## Independent evidence and recovery

Choose a small changed dataset and hand-calculate its sum, denominator, mean and percentile rank. Include tied values and zero. If no valid observations remain, report that the KPI is undefined under this contract; ledger.py rejects a normal report instead of emitting zero. Preserve your calculations for the existing NO_AI assessment policy; do not submit AI-produced arithmetic as unaided performance. Practice examples do not override that policy. Explain why these synthetic summaries establish neither citywide trends nor causal improvement.

## Runnable resources

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: (20+40+60+80)/4=50. Nearest-rank p95 uses rank ceil(.95*4)=4, hence 80. Bay means 40(n=3) and 80(n=1) have weighted mean 50, not unweighted mean 60.

lesson.title: Dashboard chart contract — labeled axes
lesson.body_md:
A chart is an argument about data, so its encoding and caption must make the underlying population clear. For a per-bay average, place the canonical bay names on the categorical axis and mean headcount per valid observation on the numeric axis. A bar chart starts its magnitude axis at zero in this exercise so bar length preserves the intended comparison. Include counts because a mean from one observation and a mean from many observations have different evidential limits.

An accessible chart does not rely on color alone. Direct labels, a text explanation and an equivalent data table let readers retrieve essential values without sight, precise color discrimination or a particular pointing device. Decorative three-dimensional bars can obscure rather than clarify the comparison.

## Guided practice

From the practice report draw two bars: bay_a mean 40 (n=3), bay_b mean 80 (n=1). Label the title “Fictional pier headcount per valid observation.” Give the axis unit and define exclusions: one missing count and one negative count were removed. Add the text table with those same values. Expected interpretation: the second observed group mean is larger in this fixture; the chart does not establish that more unique people visited that bay.

Write alt text conveying the comparison and its tiny sample rather than listing colors. A suitable explanation states that bay_a's three valid observations average 40, while bay_b's single valid observation is 80. The table carries exact values.

## Independent evidence and recovery

Produce a chart and equivalent table for the new case, tracing every plotted value to group_summary or your verified independent implementation. Ask a reviewer to recover the values using the text alternative alone. Correct clipped labels, missing units or contradictory values. A JSON flag such as chart_ok is a declaration, not a visual or accessibility review. Preserve human acceptance as pending until a reviewer actually inspects the artifact.

## Runnable resources

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: Text table: bay_a, n=3, mean=40; bay_b, n=1, mean=80. Caption: fictional observations, one missing and one negative count excluded; no unique-person or causal claim.

lesson.title: Join integrity — keys that match
lesson.body_md:
A join combines records using a key, but matching keys alone do not guarantee the intended cardinality. Each cleaned observation belongs to one bay. The metadata table must have at most one row per bay for this many-observations-to-one-label relationship. Duplicate metadata keys would multiply joined observations and can inflate aggregates.

An inner join retains only matching observations. A left join retains every observation and supplies NULL for missing metadata. Choosing an inner join without counting unmatched rows can hide data loss. The worked example uses a left join to identify orphans separately and reports the number an inner join would retain.

## Guided practice

The default metadata includes bay_a and bay_b. Expected result: inner_rows=4 and orphan_ids is empty. In a copy of ledger.py remove bay_b from DEFAULT_META, then create a new report. Expected result: inner_rows=3 and orphan_ids contains v4. The overall source report still has four cleaned observations: the join audit exposes the unmatched row instead of erasing it.

Add a duplicate bay_a metadata row in a separate copy. Expected result: a clear duplicate-metadata rejection before SQL insertion. The rule prevents an accidental fan-out; it does not resolve which real-world record would be authoritative. Restore the original file and rerun the contract tests.

## Independent evidence and recovery

Define the intended join relationship for the issued case. Include a missing key, a duplicate key and a fully matched example. Predict row counts before execution and show the actual differences. Investigate the source and metadata before modifying either; never delete an orphan solely to pass a check. Preserve the original tables, chosen policy and output for reviewer inspection. The historical lab's declared orphan count is not itself a re-execution of the join.

## Runnable resources

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: With both metadata keys, inner_rows=4 and no orphans. Remove bay_b: inner_rows=3 and orphan_ids=[v4]. A duplicate bay_a key is rejected before it can multiply rows.

weeks.title: ETL PII redaction — desks keep secrets out

lesson.title: ETL PII redaction — desks keep secrets out
lesson.body_md:
Privacy review begins before a dataset is gathered or shared. This teaching CSV contains fictional aliases and counts; do not replace them with real names, contact details, identifiers or operational records. Permission to run a local example is not permission to process institutional data.

Projection means selecting only approved columns. An exact schema can reject an unexpected email column, but approved columns can still contain private text. A filename, free-text label or precise timestamp might identify someone. Removing a name does not establish anonymity, especially for small groups. Data minimization, access control and release review address different risks.

## Guided practice

Inspect every input column and every output field. The cleaned rows retain only visit ID, normalized bay, timestamp and numeric headcount. The generated evidence also includes rejected fictional visit IDs for traceability. Expected interpretation: this is a bounded data-flow description, not an anonymization certification. Draw the path from original bytes to validated rows, summary and exported evidence. Mark where a real system would need access restrictions and retention rules.

In a local copy add a fictional email column with a value ending in example.invalid. Expected result: exact schema validation rejects the new column. Explain why a private value hidden in source_file could still evade that column-name check. Use invented text only; the example is not a PII detector.

## Independent evidence and recovery

Prepare a release review for a fictional expanded schema. Identify needed fields, unneeded fields, likely indirect identifiers, intended readers and deletion policy. Supply a redacted sample and explain what uncertainty remains. An authorized reviewer decides whether a real release is appropriate; automated booleans cannot replace that decision. If real private material appears accidentally, stop sharing it, preserve required handling evidence securely and follow the applicable institutional process.

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: An added fictional email column is rejected by the exact five-column schema. A private value placed inside an approved text column could still pass; schema validation does not prove anonymization.

weeks.title: Debug the pipeline — name the broken stage

lesson.title: Debug the pipeline — name the broken stage
lesson.body_md:
Debugging starts by distinguishing an input failure from an implementation defect. A schema mismatch, unknown alias or duplicate observation ID can be a correct rejection. An incorrect filter result for a valid input indicates a different problem. Reading the first relevant error and reproducing the smallest failing case is more useful than changing unrelated lines.

A meaningful regression test fails when a real contract violation is introduced and passes after the defect is repaired. Test outputs document behavior of specified cases. They do not prove all possible inputs correct or establish that a learner worked independently.

## Guided practice

Run all 14 public contract tests in an unchanged copy. Expected result: all pass. Then change the SQL comparison from `headcount > ?` to `headcount >= ?`. Rerun the suite. The threshold-equality case must fail because v2=40 is now wrongly selected for the strict predicate. Preserve that failing output. Repair the comparison and rerun; the test should pass again. Do not modify expected values merely to hide the defect.

Try a second defect in a separate copy: treat an empty headcount as zero. Predict which cleanup, denominator and mean checks should change. Use the named assertion and input row to explain the failure. Restore the reference before continuing.

## Independent evidence and recovery

Choose a relevant defect in your independent program, predict a test that detects it, preserve failure and repair output, and explain the root cause. Include a stage diagram: bytes → schema → cleanup → SQL → summaries → export. A file-not-found error usually needs a folder or filename correction, not a new statistical formula. Keep the original source and distinguish data repair from code repair in the journal.

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: Mutation: change > to >=. At threshold40, v2 must now wrongly appear; the strict-predicate test fails. Restore > and preserve the passing rerun alongside the failure.

lesson.title: Freshness SLA — stale tiles fail (NO_AI)
lesson.body_md:
Freshness is a defined time difference, not a decorative live badge. This model compares an explicit as-of timestamp with the newest retained valid observation. The “within policy” threshold is 30 minutes by default and includes the boundary. It is a teaching rule, not a measured service-level agreement or a guarantee of application availability.

Timestamps need explicit timezones. Two strings that display different clock hours can represent the same instant. Convert them to UTC before subtraction. A missing timezone is rejected so a local assumption does not silently change an answer. A future observation is also rejected in this model for clock and source review.

## Guided practice — calculate before running

The newest valid observation is v4 at 18:15 UTC. The missing v5 and negative v6 are not valid observations for this defined metric. At 18:40 UTC, age is 25 minutes: within the 30-minute policy. Run `ledger.py visits.csv report-stale.json --now 2026-10-01T19:00:00Z`. Expected result: age is 45 minutes and within_policy is false. This unfavorable result is correct and must remain visible.

Compare 18:40Z with 20:40+02:00 using a copied invocation. Both represent the same as-of instant, so age remains 25. Explain why a newer invalid row does not automatically make a valid-data chart fresh. Distinguish observation time from actual ingestion time; the fixture has no independently measured arrival clock.

## Independent evidence and recovery

For new case timestamps, calculate one within-policy, one exact-boundary and one stale result by hand. Preserve the canonical NO_AI assessment rules for unaided evidence. Include a missing-timezone rejection and document clock assumptions. A stale result calls for honest labeling and investigation, not changing the clock to manufacture freshness.

## Runnable resources

Open the Pier Ledger README in this course’s downloadable learner resources. Save case_data.py, ledger.py and test_ledger.py together. The guide specifies execution, expected results, troubleshooting, independent criteria and return navigation.
lesson.worked_example: As-of18:40Z minus newest-valid18:15Z gives25minutes, within30. As-of19:00Z gives45minutes, correctly stale. Neither result is a measurement of operational service availability.

weeks.title: Dashboard capstone — ship the ledger path

lesson.title: Dashboard capstone — ship the ledger path
lesson.body_md:
The capstone connects the original question to an inspectable chain of evidence. A report should make it possible to identify input bytes, transformations, selected population, formulas, join behavior, time assumptions and remaining limitations. A screenshot of a dashboard or a list of true flags cannot supply that chain by itself.

The course has a new runnable worked example and an independent variation in its Pier Ledger resources. Public tests and reference outputs are practice. The historical capstone validator checks declared fields and broad constraints; “labs_passed ≥6” alone does not independently establish that six laboratories executed or that their evidence belongs to this attempt.

## Guided practice

Reproduce the six-row example, complete the changed-threshold and stale-time runs, and retain the actual source, code version, JSON reports and test output. Build a text-first reader explanation with an accessible chart and equivalent table. Expected result: another person can trace the reported mean of 50 to four retained observations and understand both excluded rows. State that all data is fictional and no operational benefit or learner mastery was measured.

## Independent project and assessment

Use an instructor-issued seed and build your own analysis as specified in the resource guide. Deliver source bytes, source hash, code, predicted values, tests, failure-and-repair history, chart/table, privacy review and assistance disclosure. Demonstrate changed inputs in front of a reviewer where feasible. Review criteria cover source integrity, correct arithmetic and filtering, joins/time/privacy, meaningful tests, and explanation. No criterion is automatically mastered from submission or green tests.

Use the existing authorized WAIKE assignment and portfolio workflow when available; the local example does not create records or grades. Keep human review pending, revise unmet criteria, and retain earlier attempts. This project supports a learning judgment, not a credential, employment guarantee or permission to process private institutional data.
